name: The Lord's manifestations (vibhūti)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: In answer to Arjuna's question in which things the Lord is to be contemplated (10.17), he names his manifestations 'by the chief ones', since there is no end to them (10.19): the pre-eminent member of each class (10.20–38) and the seed of all beings (10.39). They are given only by way of indication (10.40); whatever being has glory, splendour or vigour springs from a portion of his splendour (10.41); and he stands supporting the whole world with one portion (10.42). Knowing this vibhūti and yoga in truth joins one to unwavering yoga (10.7).

members: the self abiding in the resting-place of all beings; their beginning, middle and end (10.20)

Uccaiḥśravas among horses; Airāvata among lordly elephants; the king among men (10.27)
the thunderbolt among weapons; the wish-yielding cow among cows; Kandarpa the begetter; Vāsuki among serpents (10.28)

the rod among subduers; policy among those seeking victory; silence among secrets; knowledge among knowers (10.38)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: At Arjuna's request (11.3–4) the Lord shows his sovereign form, which cannot be seen with ordinary sight and is seen with a divine eye (11.8): countless mouths, eyes, arms and ornaments, a radiance like a thousand suns, the whole world standing as one in his body (11.9–13), without beginning, middle or end (11.16, 11.19); the gods and seers praise it and the worlds tremble (11.20–22); the warriors of both armies rush into its mouths (11.26–30); it declares itself Time (11.32). It was shown by grace and the Lord's own yoga, never seen before by another (11.47), is not to be seen by Vedas, sacrifice, study, gifts, rites or austerity (11.48, 11.53), and is known, seen in truth and entered by undivided devotion (11.54).
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Arjuna cannot see the Lord's form with his own eye; the Lord gives him a divine eye to behold his sovereign yoga (11.8).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: The Lord declares: 'I am Time, grown mighty, the maker of the destruction of worlds, engaged here in drawing in the worlds'; even without Arjuna the opposing warriors will not survive (11.32). They are already slain by him; Arjuna is to be merely the instrument (11.33–34). Earlier he names himself time among reckoners (10.30), imperishable time (10.33) and all-seizing death (10.34); Arjuna sees the warriors enter the form's mouths like rivers into the sea and moths into a flame (11.26–30).

name: The qualities of the devotee

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: The devotee dear to the Lord: hates no being; friendly and compassionate; without 'mine' and without 'I'; the same in pain and pleasure; forbearing; ever content; self-restrained; firm in resolve; with manas and buddhi offered to him (12.13–14); neither troubling the world nor troubled by it; free of elation, impatience, fear and agitation (12.15); without expectation, pure, capable, unconcerned, free of distress, giving up all undertakings (12.16); neither rejoicing nor hating, grieving nor longing, giving up good and bad (12.17); the same to foe and friend, in honour and dishonour, cold and heat, pleasure and pain; free of attachment; equal to blame and praise; silent; content with whatever comes; without fixed abode; steady in mind (12.18–19). Those who follow this nectar of dharma with faith are exceedingly dear (12.20). Cf. the summary in 11.55 (does his work, holds him highest, devoted, unattached, without enmity).

members: yasmān nodvijate loko lokān nodvijate ca yaḥ
na hṛṣyati na dveṣṭi na śocati na kāṅkṣati
notes: The commentators divide on whether these marks describe the worshippers of the imperishable (Śaṅkara) or the devotee/relinquisher of fruits (Rāmānuja); the text calls the subject 'my devotee'.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Out of compassion the Lord gives buddhiyoga to those who worship him with love and destroys their darkness born of ignorance with the lamp of knowledge (10.10–11); he gives Arjuna the divine eye (11.8) and shows him the supreme form 'being gracious' (prasanna) by his own yoga (11.47); Arjuna asks him again and again to be gracious (11.25, 11.31, 11.44–45); he becomes before long the deliverer from the ocean of death and saṃsāra of those whose cetas has entered him (12.7).

name: The Lord in the heart of all beings

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: 'I am the self abiding in the resting-place (āśaya) of all beings; I am the beginning, middle and end of beings' (10.20).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Evenness (samatā) is among the states that arise from the Lord (10.5); the worshippers of the imperishable are even-minded everywhere (12.4); the devotee dear to the Lord is the same in pain and pleasure (12.13), to foe and friend, in honour and dishonour, cold and heat, and holds blame and praise equal (12.18–19).
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: 'Of utterances I am the single syllable' (10.25), the syllable named in 8.13 as 'om, the one-syllabled brahman'.

name: The Lord's sovereign yoga (yoga aiśvara)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: The Lord's own power, paired with his manifestation: 'this vibhūti and yoga of mine' known in truth (10.7); Arjuna asks to hear it (10.18) and to see it; with the divine eye Arjuna is to 'behold my sovereign yoga' (11.8); the supreme form was shown 'by my own yoga' (11.47). The Lord is accordingly addressed as yogin (10.17) and great lord of yoga (11.4, 11.9).

notes: Repeats 9.5 'paśya me yogam aiśvaram'. Kept distinct from the practitioner's yoga, which the same chapters also name (10.7 avikampa yoga, 12.6 ananya yoga, 12.9 abhyāsa-yoga).

name: The states of beings that arise from the Lord (BhG 10.4–5)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Twenty states (bhāva) of beings, in their several kinds, arise from the Lord alone: understanding, knowledge, freedom from delusion, forbearance, truth, restraint, calm, pleasure and pain, coming-to-be and not-being, fear and fearlessness, non-harming, evenness, contentment, austerity, giving, fame and ill-fame (10.4–5).

notes: The text does not say how they arise from him; commentators add 'according to the beings' karma'. Not the Sāṃkhya eight bhāvas.

name: Worship of the Lord and worship of the imperishable unmanifest (BhG 12.1–7)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Arjuna asks which are the better knowers of yoga: devotees ever joined who worship Kṛṣṇa, or those who worship the imperishable, the unmanifest (12.1). The Lord answers that those who fix manas on him and worship him with supreme faith are held the most joined (12.2); those who worship the imperishable — indefinable, unmanifest, all-pervading, unthinkable, unchanging, immovable, fixed — with senses restrained, even-minded, delighting in the welfare of all beings, also reach him (12.3–4), but their hardship is greater, since the unmanifest goal is reached with pain by the embodied (12.5); those who renounce all actions in him and meditate on him with undivided yoga he swiftly lifts from the ocean of death and saṃsāra (12.6–7).

notes: Later schools read this pair in terms of their own doctrines (e.g. Advaita as saguṇa/nirguṇa brahman; Viśiṣṭādvaita as the Lord vs the individual self); see dsp:bhagavad-gita-manifest-or-unmanifest-worship. The text itself uses only 'you/me' and 'the imperishable, the unmanifest'.
